title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 09–10
description: Reviewed vocabulary, conversational expressions, foods and drinks from Units 9 and 10, with British English IPA and original practice examples.

units.title: Unit 09 — Conversations 2: Useful words and expressions
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 9. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: I thought the meeting was on Friday, but it is actually on Thursday.
items.note: Actually means 'in reality', not 'at present'. It is a false friend in several languages; use currently for 'at present'.

items.example: That small restaurant is really good.
items.note: Before an adjective, really can mean very: really good or really interesting.

items.example: Would you like anything else?
items.note: Else comes after words such as anything, something, who, what and somewhere: anywhere else, what else.

items.example: Is there anything else I should bring?
items.note: Use anything else when asking whether somebody wants another thing or something additional.

items.example: The café is full, so we should go somewhere else.
items.note: Put else after somewhere to mean a different place: Let's go somewhere else.

items.example: There were around twenty people at the workshop.
items.note: Around can mean approximately when talking about times or quantities: around six o'clock; around twenty people.

items.pt: de qualquer forma; voltando ao assunto
items.example: I have to go past the station anyway, so I can give you a lift.
items.note: Anyway can explain why an action is convenient or return to an earlier topic after a digression.

items.pt: por que não fazemos...?; que tal...?
items.example: Why don’t we meet after lunch?
items.note: Make a suggestion with Why don't we + base-form verb: Why don't we go? Avoid Why don't we going?

items.example: Good idea! We can start the project together.
items.note: A positive, natural response to a suggestion. You can also say That's a good idea.

items.example: Let’s take a short break.
items.note: Make a suggestion with let's + base-form verb: Let's go. Do not say Let's going.

items.pt: tanto faz para mim; não me importo
items.example: We can walk or take the bus. I don’t mind.
items.note: Use I don't mind when either choice is acceptable. I don't mind it usually expresses lack of objection to a specific thing.

items.word: It's all the same to me
items.example: Tea or coffee? It’s all the same to me.
items.note: A conversational way to say you have no preference between the available options.

items.pt: você decide; a decisão é sua
items.example: We can leave now or later; it’s up to you.
items.note: Use It's up to you to let another person make the decision; it does not mean something is wrong.

items.example: How about having lunch outside?
items.note: To suggest an activity, use How about + -ing: How about going out? Avoid How about go.
items.speechText: How about going for a walk?

items.example: What about taking the earlier train?
items.note: Use What about + -ing for a suggestion: What about going by train? It can also introduce another topic.

items.example: Oh dear! I forgot to save the file.
items.note: A common British English reaction to surprising, worrying or disappointing news.

items.example: You can return the book tomorrow. It doesn’t matter.
items.note: Use this when something is not important or a mistake is acceptable. It requires the subject it; avoid It isn't matter.

items.example: What a pity! The exhibition closes today.
items.note: Expresses disappointment or sympathy about an unfortunate situation, not congratulations.

items.pt: muito bem!; parabéns pelo que fez!
items.example: Well done! Your presentation was excellent.
items.note: Use Well done! to praise an achievement. Well made describes how something was produced and is not a normal congratulatory reply.

items.example: Hurry up! Our bus is about to leave.
items.note: An imperative telling someone to be quick, often because there is little time.

items.example: Look out! There is a bicycle behind you.
items.note: A short, urgent warning about immediate danger. Compare Be careful!, which can be more general.

items.example: Be careful on the wet floor.
items.note: Warns someone to take care or avoid danger; it is often less urgent than Look out!

items.example: Absolutely! I think we should check it again.
items.note: An emphatic expression of agreement: Absolutely! Do not use Absolute! as a stand-alone reply.

items.example: I agree. We need more time to finish.
items.note: Agree is a verb: say I agree, not I am agree.

items.example: I don’t agree; the second option is safer.
items.note: To disagree, say I don't agree; avoid I'm not agree.

items.example: Could I make a suggestion before we decide?
items.note: A useful related expression for proposing an idea. It is a teaching extension rather than a target from the unit's vocabulary list.

items.example: We could go out for a meal after the concert.
items.note: Appears in the dialogue-correction exercise. Go out for a meal means eat somewhere away from home, usually at a restaurant.

items.example: We are going to celebrate her new job at the weekend.
items.note: Occurs in the dialogue-correction exercise. Celebrate an achievement or occasion, for example by having a meal together.

learningObjectives: Understand actually as 'in reality', use really as an intensifier, place else after suitable words, and use around for approximation.
Recognize the two conversational uses of anyway: explaining a reason and returning to an earlier topic.
Make suggestions with Why don't we + base verb, Let's + base verb, and How/What about + -ing; respond with Good idea.
Distinguish I don't mind, It's up to you and It doesn't matter in situations involving choice and importance.
Choose suitable responses such as Oh dear!, What a pity!, Well done!, Absolutely!, Hurry up!, Look out! and Be careful!.
Avoid common mistakes such as I am agree, Let's going, Why don't we going, How about go, It isn't matter and Absolute! as an agreement response.
Complete short dialogues, choose expressions appropriate to situations, and correct common errors in exercises 9.1–9.4.

units.title: Unit 10 — Food and drink
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 10. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: Healthy food can also be delicious.
items.note: Food is usually uncountable when talking about what people eat in general; foods can refer to different kinds of food.

items.example: We bought some fresh bread for breakfast.
items.note: Bread is normally uncountable: some bread, a slice of bread; not a bread when asking for an ordinary portion.

items.example: She often eats sushi for lunch.
items.note: Sushi is a Japanese food often made with rice and other ingredients. It is commonly used as an uncountable noun.

items.example: I cooked rice for the whole family.
items.note: Rice is generally uncountable: some rice, a bowl of rice; not a rice in this general meaning.

items.example: Pasta with tomato sauce is an easy dinner.
items.note: Pasta is normally uncountable when referring to food: some pasta or a plate of pasta.

items.example: This soup needs a little more salt.
items.note: Salt and pepper are common seasonings. Say put salt on chips or add salt to soup.

items.example: They shared some chips with their sandwiches.
items.note: In British English, chips are strips of fried potato; American English usually calls these fries. British crisps are American chips.

items.example: Would you like black pepper on your food?
items.note: Here, pepper refers to the seasoning, especially ground black pepper. It can also name a vegetable in other contexts.

items.example: My brother does not eat meat.
items.note: Meat is usually uncountable when it refers to food. A vegetarian does not eat meat or fish.

items.example: We are having fish and salad tonight.
items.note: Fish can refer to animals or food. It is usually uncountable when referring to the food in general.

items.example: Our guest is vegetarian, so we prepared a dish without meat.
items.note: A vegetarian is someone who does not eat meat or fish. The word may be a noun or an adjective.

items.example: I usually take sugar in my tea.
items.note: Sugar is normally uncountable. Take sugar in tea or coffee means have sugar added to the drink.

items.example: We drank tea after dinner.
items.note: Tea is normally uncountable as a drink; a tea may mean a serving in a café or restaurant.

items.example: She never drinks coffee at night.
items.note: Coffee can name the drink generally or, in an ordering context, one serving: two coffees, please.

items.pt: usar açúcar no chá ou café
items.example: Do you take sugar in your coffee?
items.note: In questions about drinks, take sugar means have sugar in your tea or coffee: Do you take sugar?

items.pt: um pouco de pão; pão (quantidade indeterminada)
items.example: Could you bring some bread to the table?
items.note: Some works with the uncountable noun bread. Avoid a bread when referring to an unspecified amount.

items.example: We sometimes eat fast food on busy days.
items.note: A general term for food prepared and served quickly; this is also the heading of section B.

items.example: Hamburgers are popular at the food festival.
items.note: The plural of hamburger is hamburgers. Hamburgers are usually made with a meat patty, though vegetarian versions exist.

items.example: The café sells hot dogs at lunchtime.
items.note: A hot dog usually has a sausage served inside a long bread roll; the plural is hot dogs.

items.example: They ordered two pizzas for the party.
items.note: The plural of pizza is pizzas. The unit groups pizzas and pasta as foods associated with Italy.

items.example: We tried fish and chips near the harbour.
items.note: A well-known dish of fried fish and fried potato chips, especially associated with Britain.

items.example: Try to eat vegetables with your main meal.
items.note: Vegetables is a plural countable noun. Compare fruit, often uncountable when naming the food category.

items.example: Fresh fruit is available at the café.
items.note: Fruit is usually uncountable when talking about fruit in general: I like fruit. Fruits can refer to kinds of fruit in other contexts.

items.example: She added carrots to the vegetable soup.
items.note: The plural of carrot is carrots. The singular is a carrot.

items.example: We planted beans in the garden.
items.note: The illustration shows long green beans in pods; beans can also refer to other kinds of bean.

items.example: The potatoes are ready to serve.
items.note: The plural of potato is potatoes, with -es. The singular is potato.

items.example: We need two tomatoes for the salad.
items.note: The plural of tomato is tomatoes, with -es. The singular is tomato.

items.example: He put some peas in the rice.
items.note: Peas is the usual plural for several small green peas. The singular is a pea.

items.example: Chop the onions before heating the oil.
items.note: Onions begins with the /ʌ/ sound, as in fun; notice the spelling does not predict an /ɒ/ sound.

items.example: I like the smell of garlic in the kitchen.
items.note: Garlic is usually uncountable when used as a cooking ingredient: some garlic, a clove of garlic.

items.example: They cooked mushrooms with rice.
items.note: The plural of mushroom is mushrooms. The unit groups them with vegetables for food vocabulary.

items.example: I ate an apple during the break.
items.note: Use an apple, because apple begins with a vowel sound.

items.example: Would you like an orange after lunch?
items.note: Orange can name a fruit or a colour; this unit uses it for the fruit. Say an orange.

items.example: He takes a banana to work every day.
items.note: In British English, banana has stress on the second syllable: /bəˈnɑːnə/.

items.example: I would like a pear, please.
items.note: Pear and pair are homophones in many British English accents.

items.example: The children shared a bowl of grapes.
items.note: Grapes is the plural of grape. A single piece is a grape.

items.example: I bought strawberries at the market.
items.note: The plural of strawberry is strawberries: change the final -y to -ies.

items.example: We cut a pineapple for dessert.
items.note: Spell this word pineapple, not pinapple or pieapple. The first part sounds like pine.

items.example: Would you like milk in your tea?
items.note: Milk is normally uncountable when it means the drink: some milk, a glass of milk.

items.example: I had fruit juice with breakfast.
items.note: Fruit juice is a two-word noun phrase for a drink made from fruit. Juice is pronounced /dʒuːs/.

items.example: The waiter brought two glasses of beer.
items.note: Beer can be uncountable as a drink or countable when ordering servings: two beers, please.

items.example: They served wine with the evening meal.
items.note: Wine is normally uncountable when talking about the drink generally; a wine may refer to a variety or serving.

items.example: Could I have a bottle of mineral water?
items.note: Mineral water is usually uncountable. You can ask for a bottle of mineral water.

items.example: Do you eat vegetables every day?
items.note: A verb used with foods: eat bread, rice, fruit or vegetables. Included as a supporting teaching extension.

items.example: What do you usually drink with dinner?
items.note: A verb used with drinks: drink water, tea, milk or juice. Included as a supporting teaching extension.

learningObjectives: Name everyday foods and drinks, including bread, rice, sushi, pasta, meat, fish, tea, milk and fruit juice.
Recognize common fast foods such as hamburgers, hot dogs, pizzas and fish and chips, and connect dishes with ingredients.
Identify and classify the illustrated fruits and vegetables using correct English names and spellings.
Use bread and fruit as generally uncountable nouns when discussing food in general; avoid a bread and fruits in these contexts.
Use take sugar in tea or coffee and describe what people eat, drink or avoid, including vegetarian diets.
Practise the British English pronunciations of fruit, vegetables, onions, pear, orange and pineapple, and spell forms such as tomatoes and pineapple.
Categorize foods, identify illustrated items, solve drink-name anagrams, and discuss personal food preferences in exercises 10.1–10.6.
